content:
The first rumor appeared in a newspaper three days after our Tuesday conversation.

AVATAR’S HOUSEHOLD EXPANDS?

I stared at the headline while the tea beside my elbow went cold.

The article contained exactly two facts.

Aang had held my hand in public.

Toph had been seen leaving Katara’s clinic after dark.

From this, the writer constructed a story involving secret ceremonies, political alliances, Air Nomad fertility law, and a sentence describing me as “an unidentified administrative companion.”

I hated that phrase most.

Toph loved it.

She burst into my office carrying three copies.

“Administrative Companion!”

“Leave.”

“Should I bow first?”

“I will file you under municipal nuisance.”

She slapped the newspaper onto my desk. “They called me mysterious.”

“They called you ‘heiress and metalbending eccentric.’”

“Still good.”

Katara arrived behind her looking far less amused.

Aang followed with the expression of a man trying very hard to practice his own philosophy about anger.

“What do we do?” I asked.

Toph sat on the corner of my desk. “Nothing.”

Katara said, “We correct the parts that could hurt people.”

Aang said, “I don’t want our relationship turned into policy.”

The room went quiet.

That was the danger beneath the ridiculous headline.

Aang was not merely a man in love. He was the Avatar. People interpreted his choices as statements even when he was choosing breakfast.

Katara was a Water Tribe hero and respected healer.

Toph was a Beifong, inventor of metalbending, and increasingly public figure in city security.

I had a desk.

Which made me, somehow, the easiest person to invent.

The article had already decided I represented nonbenders entering the Avatar’s inner circle.

Some readers would see that as hopeful.

Others would see it as proof of corruption.

Neither version had asked me who I was.

“I don’t want to hide,” Katara said.

Toph shrugged. “Then don’t.”

“I also don’t want strangers deciding they’re owed details.”

“They’re not.”

Aang paced once across the office. “If we release a statement, it becomes official.”

“It is official,” I said.

He stopped.

“Our relationship is real whether a newspaper prints it or not.”

Aang looked at me.

“That’s not what I meant.”

“I know. But I think you’re still hoping there’s a version where your private life doesn’t become public because you’re sincere enough.”

His jaw tightened.

Katara gave me a warning look.

Not because I was wrong.

Because I had struck the bruise directly.

Aang took a breath.

“You’re right.”

Toph’s head tilted.

I waited for the rest.

“I hate it,” he said.

There it was.

“I spent my childhood with monks,” he continued. “People knew me, but not like this. Then I became the Avatar and suddenly everybody thought my life was a lesson.”

Katara touched his arm.

Aang looked down at her hand.

“I don’t want loving any of you to become a lesson.”

“Then don’t teach one,” Toph said.

We all turned toward her.

She swung one foot lazily.

“Say what’s true. Nothing else.”

Katara considered that.

I did too.

An hour later, we drafted the least interesting public statement in Cranefish Town history.

Avatar Aang, Master Katara, Toph Beifong, and their partner confirmed that they were in a consensual relationship. They asked for privacy. Their personal relationship did not alter anyone’s public authority or responsibilities.

That was it.

No explanation of who kissed whom.

No declaration about marriage.

No Air Nation prophecy.

No “administrative companion.”

Toph wanted that phrase included as a joke.

We outvoted her.

The second problem was my name.

The newspapers already knew it from council records.

Using it publicly would make me easier to find.

Not using it would turn me into a mystery people could fill with anything.

“I want my name on it,” I said.

Aang looked uncertain. “Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

Katara asked, “Do you want us to say anything about your work?”

“No.”

Toph grinned. “Afraid they’ll find out how many drainage reports you’ve weaponized?”

“I have never weaponized a drainage report.”

“You hit a councilman with one.”

“I gestured emphatically.”

“With forty pages.”

Katara laughed.

The statement went out that afternoon.

By evening, six newspapers had printed it.

By the next morning, street vendors were selling cheap sketches of the four of us that looked nothing like any of us.

Toph bought one.

“Why?” I asked.

“They gave me huge arms.”

“They gave Aang a mustache.”

Aang looked offended. “I could grow one.”

Katara stared at him.

“No,” she said.

“You don’t know that.”

“I know enough.”

The public reaction was not entirely funny.

A letter arrived at the council office accusing me of distracting the Avatar from his duty.

Another called Katara immoral.

A third praised Toph for “refusing conventional domesticity,” which made her mutter that strangers were somehow annoying even when they agreed with her.

One letter asked whether Aang planned to restore Air Nomad polygamy.

He read it twice.

“I don’t know if that was ever a thing.”

“Does it matter?” I asked.

“It matters if people are inventing my culture to explain me.”

That one hurt him.

I could see it.

He spent the afternoon in the temple room he had built above the house, meditating beneath old Air Nomad carvings. I did not follow immediately.

Katara did not either.

“Give him a little time,” she said.

Toph’s foot tapped the floor.

“He hates when dead people get turned into costumes.”

The bluntness was pure Toph.

It was also exactly right.

When I finally climbed the stairs, Aang was seated before a small statue of Gyatso.

I sat near the door.

He opened his eyes.

“I’m sorry,” I said.

“For what?”

“For the world being terrible at boundaries.”

Aang smiled faintly.

“That isn’t yours to apologize for.”

“I know. I’m practicing Katara.”

He laughed.

I moved closer.

“Do you regret saying it publicly?”

“No.”

“Do you regret us?”

Aang’s expression sharpened.

“No.”

The answer was immediate enough to settle something in me.

He held out his hand.

I took it.

“We’re going to get things wrong,” he said.

“Obviously. Toph is involved.”

From downstairs came a muffled shout: “I heard that!”

Aang laughed so hard he lost his meditative posture.

Katara called up, “Dinner!”

Aang squeezed my hand.

We went downstairs together.

The world knew now.

Not the private shape of us.

Not the things that belonged only to four people around a table.

But enough.

At dinner, Toph propped the terrible newspaper sketch against the teapot.

Aang’s drawn mustache curled nearly to his ears.

Katara had been given a crown.

Toph looked like she could bench-press a badgermole.

I had been drawn holding a scroll.

“Honestly,” Toph said, “they nailed Paperwork.”

I threw a dumpling at her.

She caught it in her mouth.

Public life could have the headline.

It could not have the way Aang’s knee pressed against mine under the table, or the way Katara automatically split the last sweet bun into four pieces, or the way Toph slid the largest piece onto my plate when she thought no one noticed.

Those things remained ours.

The newspaper did not stop printing stories because we refused to feed them.

For a week, strangers developed opinions about which of us Aang “really” loved, whether Katara was secretly heartbroken, whether Toph had coerced anyone, and—my personal favorite—whether I was an elaborate political symbol invented by the council.

“I knew you were suspicious,” Toph said when I read that one aloud.

“I’m devastated to learn I don’t exist.”

Katara folded the paper into a neat square. “Stop reading them.”

“You read them.”

“I read them so I know what people are saying.”

“That is different because?”

“Because I said it more confidently.”

Aang laughed into his sleeve.

The humor helped, but not enough.

That afternoon, a woman stopped me outside the public records office and asked which of them I preferred.

I stared at her.

She waited as if this were reasonable.

“Do you ask parents which child is real?” I said finally.

Her face changed.

I regretted the comparison immediately—relationships were not children, and love did not become moral simply because there was more than one person involved—but the question had done what I needed. It interrupted her certainty.

When I told the others later, Katara said, “You don’t owe strangers a lesson every time they’re rude.”

Toph added, “Sometimes you can just say none of your business.”

Aang considered this. “Could I say that as the Avatar?”

“Yes,” three of us answered.

He looked delighted.

The next headline called him evasive.

Toph framed it.

The framed headline eventually hung in the hallway. Beneath it, I added a second clipping: AVATAR DECLINES TO COMMENT ON PRIVATE HOUSEHOLD MATTERS.

Toph declared it an improvement.

Aang looked absurdly proud of himself.

Katara said nothing, but I caught her smiling every time she passed it.

Eventually the hallway wall became a joke only we understood: evidence that public certainty could be loud, wrong, and still less important than what happened at our table.

That mattered more than anything they printed.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
